content: The document outlines a comprehensive framework for assessing and improving COVID-19 vaccination programs, focusing on various behavioral, social, and logistical factors that influence vaccine uptake. Below is a professional interpretation of the content: 1. Administrative Data Collection: Interviewers are required to record the date of the interview, participant ID, and location details (e.g., GPS coordinates, cluster number, district name). The area type (rural or urban) is also noted to adapt the survey methodology accordingly. 2. Informed Consent: Participants are informed about the purpose of the survey, which is to improve vaccination services in their country. Participation is voluntary and anonymous, and respondents can skip questions or stop the interview at any time. Consent is obtained before proceeding. 3. Demographic Information: Age: Respondents are asked their age in completed years to allow stratified analysis by age groups, such as 18–34 years or 55+ years. Gender: Gender identity is recorded to enable stratified analysis. In contexts where third-gender categories are culturally recognized, these options can be included. Occupation: Respondents are asked about their work during the pandemic (e.g., health workers, essential service workers) to identify priority occupational groups and stratify data accordingly. 4. Health and COVID-19 History: Chronic Conditions: Respondents are asked if they have any chronic conditions (e.g., obesity, diabetes, lung disease) to identify those at higher risk and prioritize vaccination. COVID-19 Diagnosis: Respondents are asked if they have had COVID-19, whether it was mild or severe, and if it was confirmed by a test. This helps assess how prior infection influences vaccination intentions. 5. Vaccination Intentions and Perceptions: Intent to Vaccinate: Respondents are asked if they want to receive a COVID-19 vaccine if recommended by a medical professional. Those who decline can provide reasons in an open-text format. Perceived Importance: Respondents are asked how important they believe vaccination is for their health, assessing positive attitudes toward vaccination. Perceived Safety: Respondents are asked how safe they believe the vaccine is, addressing concerns about potential harm. Social Motivations: Questions assess whether respondents believe vaccination will allow them to safely see family and friends again. 6. Social and Community Influences: Peer Norms: Respondents are asked if they think most adults they know will get vaccinated if recommended. Workplace Norms: Respondents are asked if they believe most of their colleagues will get vaccinated. Family and Religious Leader Influence: Questions assess whether close family, friends, or religious leaders encourage vaccination. Community Leader Influence: Respondents are asked if community leaders support vaccination. 7. Health Worker Influence: Respondents are asked if a health worker has recommended vaccination. This includes advice given during clinic visits or reminders about being due for vaccination. 8. Access and Availability: Recall Systems: Respondents are asked if they have been contacted about being due for vaccination, assessing the effectiveness of reminder systems. Travel Autonomy: Respondents are asked if they need permission to leave home to get vaccinated, with data stratified by gender to assess women’s travel autonomy. Knowledge of Vaccination Sites: Respondents are asked if they know where to go to get vaccinated. On-Site Vaccination: Health workers are asked if vaccines are available at their workplace. 9. Ease of Access and Affordability: Ease of Access: Respondents are asked how easy it is to get vaccinated, considering logistical challenges. Affordability: Respondents are asked how easy it is to pay for vaccination, including associated costs like transportation and time off work. 10. Barriers to Access: Respondents are asked what makes it difficult to get vaccinated, with multiple response options such as vaccine unavailability, difficulty making appointments, inconvenient site locations or hours, long waiting times, inability to leave work, or being turned away without vaccination. 11. Service Satisfaction and Quality: Satisfaction: Respondents are asked how satisfied they are with vaccination services, focusing on their experience during their last visit. Quality Issues: Respondents are asked what aspects of the service were unsatisfactory, such as vaccine unavailability, long waiting times, unclean facilities, poorly trained or disrespectful staff, or rushed interactions. 12. Staff Competence and Respect: Questions assess perceptions of staff training, respectfulness, and the time spent with patients. These factors influence trust and satisfaction with vaccination services. This framework provides a detailed approach to understanding the factors influencing COVID-19 vaccination uptake, enabling tailored interventions to address barriers and improve service delivery.
